6                      UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                       
7                                                                         
                      NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA                     
8                                                                         

9                                                                         

10    JAMIE POSTPICHAL, et al.,                                            
11             Plaintiffs,              No.  C 19–07270 WHA                

12         v.                                                              
                                       ORDER GRANTING MOTION              
13    CRICKET WIRELESS, LLC,            TO DISMISS CLRA CLAIMS             
14             Defendant.                                                  

15                                                                         
16                                                                         
17        California’s Consumer Legal Remedies Act bans certain practices that the California 
18    legislature has deemed to be “unfair” or “deceptive.”  Plaintiffs allege claims under CLRA 
19    Sections 1170(a)(5), (7), and (9), which prohibit misleading representations and 
20    advertisements.  Plaintiffs filed this lawsuit with CLRA claims for injunctive relief only, 
21    waited 30 days, then amended their complaint to include damages claims.  Plaintiffs have not 
22    alleged that a CLRA notice was sent to Cricket with regard to this matter prior to amending the 
23    complaint to include damages.                                        
24        CLRA has a specific notice requirement set out in 1782(d):       

25             An action for injunctive relief brought under the specific  
              provisions of Section 1770 may be commenced without         
26             compliance with subdivision (a).  Not less than 30 days after the 
              commencement of an action for injunctive relief, and after  
27             compliance with subdivision (a), the consumer may amend his or 
              her complaint without leave of court to include a request for 
              be applicable if the complaint for injunctive relief is amended to 
1             request damages.                                            
2    Subdivision (a) requires:                                            

3             (a)  Thirty days or more prior to the commencement of an action 
              for damages pursuant to this title, the consumer shall do the 
4             following:                                                  

5                  (1)  Notify the person alleged to have employed or     
              committed methods, acts, or practices declared unlawful by  
6             Section 1770 of the particular alleged violations of Section 1770. 

7                  (2)  Demand that the person correct, repair, replace, or 
              otherwise rectify the goods or services alleged to be in violation of 
8             Section 1770.                                               

9             The notice shall be in writing and shall be sent by certified or 
              registered mail, return receipt requested, to the place where the 
10             transaction occurred or to the person's principal place of business 
              within California.                                          
11                                                                         
12        Plaintiffs have not fulfilled this notice requirement.  The initiation of the lawsuit itself 
13    does not provide notice under subdivision (a).  Plaintiffs lean on a prior CLRA notice sent to 
14    Cricket in 2015 in a case that was subsequently dismissed.  Though the claimant would be a 
15    member of the proposed class and the claims there paralleled the present claims, that notice 
16    arose from a different lawsuit long before the initiation of this matter.  This does not satisfy 
17    CLRA’s requirement because that notice did not involve “the consumer[s]” who have brought 
18    the current claims.                                                  
19        Nor does the fact that Cricket received general complaints from consumers prior to the 
20    filing of this lawsuit (including putative class members that are not putative class 
21    representatives) satisfy CLRA’s notice requirement either.           
22        While Cricket cannot credibly claim that it was not on actual notice of the bad acts herein 
23    alleged, the legislative intent of Section 1782(d) — allowing time for defendants to correct 
24    violations in light of the specter of a CLRA lawsuit before plaintiffs pursue damages — serves 
25    a vital role in promoting efficient resolution of alleged CLRA violations.  Whether Cricket 
26    would correct its violations with notice at this point seems unlikely, but the procedural 
27    requirements set out by CLRA are unyielding and must be followed.    
    1          The failure to give notice does not render plaintiffs’ claims unrevivable.  The California 
    2      court of appeal has held: 
    3                [The notice] requirement exists in order to allow a defendant to 
                    avoid liability for damages if the defendant corrects the alleged 
    4                wrongs within 30 days after notice, or indicates within that 30-day 
                    period that it will correct those wrongs within a reasonable time. 
    5                A dismissal with prejudice of a damages claim filed without the 
                    requisite notice is not required to satisfy this purpose.  Instead, the 
    6                claim must simply be dismissed until 30 days or more after the 
                    plaintiff complies with the notice requirements.  If, before that 
    7                30-day period expires the defendant corrects the alleged wrongs or 
                    indicates it will correct the wrongs, the defendant cannot be held 
    8                liable for damages. 
    9      Morgan v. AT&T Wireless Servs., Inc., 177 Cal. App. 4th 1235, 1261 (2009). 
   10          Mazza v. Am. Honda Motor Co. reversed a  district court’s blanket application of CLRA 
   11      to out of state class members, acknowledging that “foreign states have a strong interest in the 
    12      application of their laws to transactions between their citizens and corporations doing business 

     13      within their state” and holding that “each class member's consumer protection claim should be 

 v   14      governed by the consumer protection laws of the jurisdiction in which the transaction took 

    15      place.”  666 F.3d 581, 594 (9th Cir. 2012).  If plaintiffs give notice and decide to file a new 
A    16      CLRA action, plaintiffs should be aware that the undersigned is unlikely to permit out-of-state 


    17      plaintiffs to submit CLRA claims. 

4    18          Plaintiffs’ CLRA claims are DISMISSED.  A further order on the motion to dismiss 
   19      plaintiffs’ RICO claims is forthcoming. 
   20 
   21          IT IS SO ORDERED. 
   22 
   23      Dated:  June 7, 2021 
   24

   %6                                                   ILLIAM ALSUP 
                                                     UNITED STATES DISTRICT  JUDGE
